questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}2{x}^{2}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)$ for $\,1\le x\le 2e?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(t).$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)⟩,\,1\le t\le 2e
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(t))j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{t}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}{e}^{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2{t}^{2}\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2e}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2e}2{t}^{3}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2e}{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y={x}^{3}$ between the points $(0,0)$ and $(2,8)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)={t}^{3}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,{t}^{3}⟩,\,0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})j \\  & =i+3{t}^{2}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+9{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =t\cdot {t}^{3}={t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{4}\sqrt{1+9{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=2{e}^{x}$ for $\,0\le x\le 2?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=2{e}^{t}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,2{e}^{t}⟩,\,0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t})j \\  & =i+2{e}^{t}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(2{e}^{t})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{e}^{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+4{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+4{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}2{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=\frac{1}{x}$ between the points $(1,1)$ and $(2,\frac{1}{2})?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\frac{1}{t}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\frac{1}{t}⟩,\,1\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+1}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2{x}^{3}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\cdot {t}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{t}=2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+1}}{{t}^{2}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}y{e}^{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=5x+2$ for $\,0\le x\le 1?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=5t+2.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,5t+2⟩,\,0\le t\le 1
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+2)j \\  & =i+5\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{26}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y{e}^{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(5t+2){e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(5t+2){e}^{t}\cdot \sqrt{26}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{26}{\int }_{0}^{1}(5t+2){e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=2xy$ along the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}},$ $\,0\le x\le 2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}⟩,\,0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}})j \\  & =i-\frac{t}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(-\frac{t}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4-{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2t\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2t\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}\cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2({2}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=2{y}^{2}$ along the curve $y={e}^{x},$ $\,0\le x\le \operatorname{ln}⁡3.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)={e}^{t}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,{e}^{t}⟩,\,0\le t\le \operatorname{ln}⁡3
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})j \\  & =i+{e}^{t}j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2({e}^{t})^{2}=2{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{2t}\cdot \sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{2t}\,\sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+{e}^{2t}$, $\text{d}u=2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}2{e}^{2t}\,\sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{2}^{10}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{2}^{10} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({10}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(10\sqrt{10}-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}(5\sqrt{10}-\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4},$ $\,0\le x\le 4\sqrt{6}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}⟩,\,0\le t\le 4\sqrt{6}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{2}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(\frac{t}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})}{t}=\frac{t}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}\frac{t}{4}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}t\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}$, $\text{d}u=\frac{t}{2}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}t\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{25}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{3}{|}_{1}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({25}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(125-1) \\  & =\frac{124}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x-y}$ along the line $y=x-4,$ $\,0\le x\le 2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=t-4.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,t-4⟩,\,0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4)j \\  & =i+\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x-y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{t-(t-4))}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\,t\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(2-0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=({x}^{2}+y)$ along the line $y=3x+2,$ $\,0\le x\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=3t+2.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,3t+2⟩,\,0\le t\le 1
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2)j \\  & =i+3\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={t}^{2}+(3t+2)={t}^{2}+3t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+3t+2)\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+3t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}\,(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}+2t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{10}(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{3}{2}+2) \\  & =\frac{23\sqrt{10}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} \dfrac{y^2}{x} \,\textrm ds,
$$

 where $C$ is the section of the curve $y = \dfrac{x^3}3$ between the points $(0,0)$ and $(3,9).$
Write the line integral in the form 

$$
\displaystyle\int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y = y(t) = \dfrac{t^3}{3}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, \dfrac{t^3}3 \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 3,
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3})j \\  & =i+{t}^{2}\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{({t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y^2}{x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{{(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3})}^{2}}{t}=\frac{1}{9}{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{9}{t}^{5}\cdot \sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{5}\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \dfrac{y^3}{x^2} \, \text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is given by $y = x$ for $\, 0 \le x \le 4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y = y(t) = t.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, \: t \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 4
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y^3}{x^2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{{t}^{3}}{{t}^{2}}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}t\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{4}t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}({4}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =8\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
